pros: Excellent average-case performance: O(n log n) with small constant factor
In-place sorting: O(log n) auxiliary space for recursion stack
Fewer comparisons and swaps than Heap Sort in practice
Hoare partitioning does approximately n/3 swaps (very efficient)
Can be optimized with hybrid approaches (Introsort, median-of-three)
Empirically fastest comparison-based sort for most datasets
Three-way partitioning variant handles duplicates efficiently
Foundation for QuickSelect (selection in O(n) average time)
Simple inner loop enables good compiler optimization
Dominates standard library implementations (C++, Java primitives, Rust, Go)
cons: O(n²) worst-case time complexity with naive pivot selection
Not stable: does not preserve order of equal elements
Recursive implementation risks stack overflow on worst-case input
Performance heavily dependent on pivot quality
Degrades to O(n²) on already-sorted arrays with first/last element pivot
Not adaptive: cannot exploit partially sorted input
More comparisons than Merge Sort (~1.39 vs 1.00 n log n)
Random pivot adds overhead of random number generation
Partitioning logic is error-prone and hard to implement correctly
Requires random access (not suitable for linked lists)
Branch mispredictions on modern CPUs can impact performance
Standard implementations often switch to insertion sort for small n
